arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on SSA construction and alias analysis, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.
arguments.instructions:
Write two sections.

SECTION 1: SSA construction. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Cytron et al.'s dominance-frontier-based phi-insertion algorithm (iterated dominance frontiers, dominator tree construction via Lengauer-Tarjan)
- The "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form" (Braun et al.) algorithm using local value numbering + incomplete phis + phi simplification during traversal
- Semi-pruned/pruned SSA and minimal SSA distinctions, and why liveness-based pruning reduces phi count
- SSA destruction mechanisms: dead phi elimination, copy insertion and the phi-swap/lost-copy/parallel-copy problems at merge points, and the sequentialization algorithm for resolving parallel copies
Explain mechanism, data structures, complexity, correctness invariants (dominance property, single-assignment property).

SECTION 2: Alias analysis. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis (subset constraints, worklist-based fixpoint, cubic complexity)
- Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis (equality constraints, union-find, near-linear complexity) and the precision/speed tradeoff vs Andersen's
- Type-based alias analysis (TBAA), as used in LLVM, using type system guarantees (e.g. strict aliasing rules in C/C++) to disambiguate
- Flow-sensitive vs flow-insensitive, context-sensitive vs context-insensitive distinctions; also mention may-alias vs must-alias, and the use of alias sets / memory SSA for optimization scheduling

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text.

arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on register allocation and instruction scheduling, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.
arguments.instructions:
Write two sections.

SECTION 1: Register allocation. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Graph-coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs style): interference graph construction, the simplify-spill-select worklist algorithm, optimistic coloring, Briggs' conservative coalescing vs Chaitin's coalescing, spill cost heuristics
- Linear scan register allocation: live interval computation, the Poletto-Sarkar algorithm, active/inactive interval lists, use for JIT compilers (why speed matters there)
- SSA-based/graph-coloring-on-SSA allocation: chordal interference graphs under SSA and the Hack/Pereira/Palsberg results enabling allocation without full graph coloring
- Spilling and rematerialization strategies; live range splitting; second-chance binpacking
Explain complexity, correctness invariants, and tradeoffs (compile time vs code quality).

SECTION 2: Instruction scheduling. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- List scheduling with priority functions over a data dependence DAG (true/anti/output dependencies), critical path and the use of scheduling priorities like latency-weighted depth
- Software pipelining, specifically modulo scheduling (iterative modulo scheduling, resource and recurrence minimum initiation intervals MII_res/MII_rec)
- Trace scheduling and superblock/hyperblock scheduling for VLIW, including compensation code
- Local vs global (regional) scheduling, list scheduling vs. the Sethi-Ullman style scheduling for expression trees, and the interaction between scheduling and register allocation (register pressure-aware scheduling)

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text.

arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on inlining and escape analysis, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.
arguments.instructions:
Write two sections.

SECTION 1: Inlining. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Cost-benefit heuristic inlining (as in GCC/LLVM): size growth thresholds, call-site frequency weighting via profile data, inline cost models
- Profile-guided inlining / PGO-directed inlining using edge and block execution counts to prioritize hot call sites
- Bottom-up vs top-down inlining order, and the use of a call graph with an inlining worklist; handling of recursive calls and recursion depth limits
- Partial inlining and inline cloning, specialization (e.g. via cloning for constant arguments), and devirtualization as an enabler of inlining (speculative devirtualization with guards)
Explain the algorithms, heuristics, and correctness considerations (e.g. semantic preservation, exception handling across inlined boundaries).

SECTION 2: Escape analysis. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Connection graph / points-to based escape analysis (as in the Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira algorithm used in Java JITs), classifying objects as NoEscape/ArgEscape/GlobalEscape
- Abstract interpretation-based / flow-sensitive intraprocedural escape analysis with interprocedural summary propagation
- Scalar replacement of aggregates enabled by escape analysis (turning non-escaping heap objects into SSA scalar values / stack-allocated fields)
- Stack allocation conversion of non-escaping objects, and lock elision/synchronization removal enabled by thread-escape analysis (determining an object is thread-local)

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text.

arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on loop vectorization and general loop optimizations, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.
arguments.instructions:
Write two sections.

SECTION 1: Loop vectorization. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Loop-level (classic) vectorization via dependence analysis: distance/direction vectors, the GCD test and Banerjee's test for determining loop-carried dependencies, and legality criteria for transforming scalar loops to SIMD
- Superword-Level Parallelism (SLP) vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe): building isomorphic statement packs bottom-up from independent scalar statements rather than whole loops
- Loop unroll-and-jam combined with vectorization, strip-mining to generate vector-width chunks, and handling of loop remainders/epilogues
- Vectorization of reductions (handling associative/commutative reduction idioms), and masked/predicated vectorization for handling control flow inside loops (if-conversion)

SECTION 2: Loop optimizations. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth, e.g.:
- Loop-invariant code motion (LICM), using dominance to hoist invariant computations out of loop bodies, interaction with speculative hoisting and PRE (partial redundancy elimination)
- Loop unrolling (full vs partial) and its effect on branch overhead and ILP; strength reduction of induction variables (replacing multiplications with additions using linear function test replacement)
- Loop fusion and loop fission/distribution, loop interchange for improving cache locality (reordering nested loops based on the memory access stride / reuse distance), and loop tiling/blocking for cache-aware blocking of iteration space
- Loop-invariant guard elimination, loop peeling, and induction variable canonicalization (canonical induction variables for simplifying bound/step analysis)

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text.

messages.content: I can only run 3 children at once, so I'll cover all 8 areas by merging SSA construction and alias analysis into the frontend child's workload alongside register allocation/scheduling in the backend child, and keep inlining/escape analysis and loop vectorization/loop optimizations as the other two. Let me consolidate into exactly 3 spawns.

arguments.instructions:
Write two sections, SSA construction and alias analysis.

SECTION 1: SSA construction. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth:
- Cytron et al.'s dominance-frontier-based phi-insertion algorithm (iterated dominance frontiers, dominator tree construction via Lengauer-Tarjan)
- The "Simple and Efficient Construction of SSA Form" (Braun et al.) algorithm using local value numbering + incomplete phis + phi simplification during traversal
- Semi-pruned/pruned SSA vs minimal SSA distinctions, and why liveness-based pruning reduces phi count
- SSA destruction: dead phi elimination, copy insertion, the phi-swap/lost-copy/parallel-copy problems at merge points, and sequentialization of parallel copies
Explain mechanism, data structures, complexity, correctness invariants (dominance property, single-assignment property).

SECTION 2: Alias analysis. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth:
- Andersen's inclusion-based points-to analysis (subset constraints, worklist-based fixpoint, cubic complexity)
- Steensgaard's unification-based points-to analysis (equality constraints, union-find, near-linear complexity) and the precision/speed tradeoff vs Andersen's
- Type-based alias analysis (TBAA), as used in LLVM, using strict-aliasing type system guarantees to disambiguate
- Flow-sensitive vs flow-insensitive and context-sensitive vs context-insensitive distinctions; may-alias vs must-alias; alias sets / memory SSA for optimization scheduling

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text of both sections.
arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on SSA construction and alias analysis, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.

arguments.instructions:
Write two sections, register allocation and instruction scheduling.

SECTION 1: Register allocation. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth:
- Graph-coloring register allocation (Chaitin-Briggs style): interference graph construction, simplify-spill-select worklist algorithm, optimistic coloring, Briggs' conservative coalescing vs Chaitin's coalescing, spill cost heuristics
- Linear scan register allocation: live interval computation, the Poletto-Sarkar algorithm, active/inactive interval lists, use in JIT compilers
- SSA-based allocation: chordal interference graphs under SSA and Hack/Pereira/Palsberg results enabling allocation without full graph coloring
- Spilling and rematerialization strategies, live range splitting, second-chance binpacking
Explain complexity, correctness invariants, and tradeoffs (compile time vs code quality).

SECTION 2: Instruction scheduling. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth:
- List scheduling with priority functions over a data dependence DAG (true/anti/output dependencies), critical path, latency-weighted depth priorities
- Software pipelining via modulo scheduling (iterative modulo scheduling, resource and recurrence minimum initiation intervals MII_res/MII_rec)
- Trace scheduling and superblock/hyperblock scheduling for VLIW, including compensation code
- Local vs global/regional scheduling, Sethi-Ullman scheduling for expression trees, register-pressure-aware scheduling

Use precise standard terminology. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text of both sections.
arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on register allocation and instruction scheduling, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.

arguments.instructions:
Write four sections: inlining, escape analysis, loop vectorization, loop optimizations.

SECTION 1: Inlining. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth: cost-benefit heuristic inlining (size thresholds, profile-weighted call-site prioritization, inline cost models as in GCC/LLVM); PGO-directed inlining using edge/block execution counts; bottom-up vs top-down inlining order using a call graph worklist, recursion depth limits; partial inlining, inline cloning, specialization via cloning for constant args, and devirtualization (including speculative devirtualization with guards) as an inlining enabler. Discuss correctness considerations (semantic preservation, exception handling across inlined boundaries).

SECTION 2: Escape analysis. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth: connection graph / points-to based escape analysis (Choi/Gupta/Midkiff/Moreira), classifying objects NoEscape/ArgEscape/GlobalEscape; flow-sensitive intraprocedural escape analysis with interprocedural summary propagation; scalar replacement of aggregates enabled by escape analysis; stack allocation conversion of non-escaping objects and lock elision via thread-escape analysis.

SECTION 3: Loop vectorization. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth: loop-level vectorization via dependence analysis (distance/direction vectors, GCD test, Banerjee's test, legality criteria); Superword-Level Parallelism (SLP) vectorization (Larsen & Amarasinghe) building isomorphic statement packs; unroll-and-jam with strip-mining and remainder/epilogue loops; vectorization of reductions and masked/predicated vectorization via if-conversion.

SECTION 4: Loop optimizations. Cover at least three named mechanisms in depth: loop-invariant code motion (LICM) using dominance, interaction with PRE; loop unrolling (full/partial) and induction variable strength reduction (linear function test replacement); loop fusion/fission, loop interchange for cache locality, loop tiling/blocking; loop peeling and canonical induction variable introduction.

Use precise standard terminology throughout. Be technically exhaustive, not a shallow survey. Return the full written text of all four sections.
arguments.objective: Produce rigorous technical sub-briefs on inlining, escape analysis, loop vectorization, and loop optimizations, each covering at least three specific named mechanisms in depth.
